finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST 'feed' parameter is passed to file_get_contents, so any remote client can make the server fetch an arbitrary URL. Only strlen of the response is echoed, so this is blind SSRF with a length oracle. file:// is also accepted by the wrapper.
finding.source: import.php:11 - $_POST['feed'], supplied by any remote client. The only gate is REQUEST_METHOD === 'POST' and isset($_POST['feed']). No session or admin check.
finding.sink: import.php:12 - file_get_contents($_POST['feed']), an outbound HTTP/HTTPS/FTP request or local stream read chosen by the attacker.

trace.note: session_start() runs, but nothing on this branch checks the session.
Branch entered for any POST with a feed field. No require_admin, no scheme or host allowlist, no private-IP check.
Raw attacker string passed to file_get_contents, which fetches it and follows redirects by default.
Only strlen of the body is echoed. Blind SSRF with a length side channel.

finding.guards_checked: None on the path. No parse_url or scheme/host allowlist, no check for loopback, RFC1918 or link-local addresses such as 169.254.169.254, no redirect re-validation, no timeout or size cap. Exploitability assumes allow_url_fopen is enabled, the PHP default; the repo does not set it.

verdict.guard_found: none. import.php:11 gates only on REQUEST_METHOD === 'POST' and isset($_POST['feed']). require_admin() (import.php:4-9) is defined but not called on this branch; it runs only at line 18 under set_webhook. The value goes unvalidated into file_get_contents at line 12, and only strlen of the result is echoed at line 13.
verdict.reason: import.php:11-12 passes the unauthenticated $_POST['feed'] straight to file_get_contents with no session, admin, scheme, or host check, and import.php:13 echoes only the length, so the trace holds as a blind SSRF with a length oracle. The file:// claim is also consistent with PHP's file_get_contents, though http(s) fetches depend on allow_url_fopen, as the candidate notes.

finding.claim: An admin-authenticated POST set_webhook value is passed to curl_init and curl_exec, so an admin can make the server issue requests to arbitrary URLs. The response body is discarded, so the request is blind. Lower severity because the caller must be admin.
finding.source: import.php:19 - $_POST['set_webhook'], supplied by a client with an admin session. The admin gate is require_admin() at import.php:18, which checks only that $_SESSION['is_admin'] is non-empty.
finding.sink: import.php:20-22 - curl_init($hook) and curl_exec($ch), an outbound request to the attacker-chosen URL.

trace.note: Branch entered when set_webhook is present.
require_admin() called; exits 403 if is_admin is empty (lines 4-9).
POST value copied to $hook with no validation.
curl_exec runs the request. RETURNTRANSFER is set but the body is discarded.

finding.guards_checked: Session flag check only. The flag is set outside this file, so how it is assigned could not be verified. No URL validation. CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION is not set, so redirects are not followed. libcurl still accepts schemes such as gopher://, file:// and dict://.

verdict.guard_found: require_admin() at import.php:4-9 and its call at import.php:18. It checks only that $_SESSION['is_admin'] is non-empty, so it is not a closing guard. The source is still admin-only.
verdict.reason: Every trace line (import.php:17-23) matches the code, but the value reaching curl_init at import.php:19-20 comes from $_POST['set_webhook'], which is reachable only after require_admin() at import.php:18 passes, so the source is admin-only and not controllable by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker. The candidate itself rates this as lower severity for that reason. Whether the is_admin flag can be set by a low-privilege user depends on code outside this file, which I could not check, so that remains an open question rather than a confirmed path.
